article_title: Computer Anxiety in E-Learning: The Effect of Computer Self-Efficacy
citation: Saadé, R. G., & Kira, D. (2009). Computer Anxiety in E-Learning: The Effect of Computer Self-Efficacy. Journal of Information Technology Education, 8. https://jite.org/documents/Vol8/JITEv8p177-191Saade708.pdf
title: Design LMSs with simple, interactive, familiar features to reduce anxiety and leverage self-efficacy mediation
description: The authors recommend that designers "integrate simple, interactive, and familiar features in the design of LMSs" and provide incentives to motivate usage, because positive learning experiences are more likely with LMSs that are easy to use and introduce the least anxieties. This assists diffusion via the mediating effect of computer self-efficacy. They also note a trade-off: easier interfaces may reduce effective task manipulation capabilities.
requirements: Designers must balance ease of navigation against effective task manipulation (the cognitive-cost/effective-usage ratio)
constraints: The more 'easy to use' the interface is designed, the less effective the features become, reducing LMS capabilities
target_learning_goals: supporting positive attitudes and ease of use perceptions in LMS-based learning
examples: The authors suggest it is feasible to build multiple LMS interfaces for students with different levels of computer self-efficacy
key_sources: Saadé, R. G., & Kira, D. (2009). Computer Anxiety in E-Learning: The Effect of Computer Self-Efficacy. Journal of Information Technology Education, 8. https://jite.org/documents/Vol8/JITEv8p177-191Saade708.pdf

article_title: On opportunities and challenges of large multimodal foundation models in education
citation: Küchemann, S., Avila, K. E., Dinc, Y., Hortmann, C., Revenga, N., Ruf, V., Stausberg, N., Steinert, S., Fischer, F., Fischer, M., Kasneci, E., Kasneci, G., Kuhr, T., Kutyniok, G., Malone, S., Sailer, M., Schmidt, A., Stadler, M., Weller, J. & Kuhn, J. (2025). On opportunities and challenges of large multimodal foundation models in education. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00301-w
title: Large multimodal foundation models (LMFMs) as LLM-enabled multimodal AI middleware for education
description: LMFMs are foundation models that, building on the LLM-as-middleware idea demonstrated by Shen and colleagues, process inputs and outputs not only via written text but also via spoken text, images, and videos, with examples ChatGPT-4-Turbo and Gemini. The review frames them as advancing personalized learning, engagement, and research tooling, while raising accuracy, bias, privacy, and access concerns. It characterizes them as representing "a significant advancement in this field due to its multimodality, boosted accuracy, faster response times". The framework organizes the article's four-audience analysis of opportunities and challenges.
requirements: Requires LLMs fine-tuned to the specifications of connected AI tools to generate correct inputs, per the middleware account.
Educational use requires reevaluation of teaching methods, curricula, and new competencies among educators and students, per the review.
constraints: Accuracy and reliability of outputs remain concerns; biases may be intensified by processing multiple input modalities.
The digital divide and resource limits of educational institutions constrain equitable implementation, per the review.
examples: The review describes LMFM capabilities including speech-to-text, image-to-text, text-to-image, and text-to-speech functionalities supporting barrier-free interaction for students with disabilities.
key_sources: Küchemann, S., Avila, K. article_title: On opportunities and challenges of large multimodal foundation models in education
citation: Küchemann, S., Avila, K. E., Dinc, Y., Hortmann, C., Revenga, N., Ruf, V., Stausberg, N., Steinert, S., Fischer, F., Fischer, M., Kasneci, E., Kasneci, G., Kuhr, T., Kutyniok, G., Malone, S., Sailer, M., Schmidt, A., Stadler, M., Weller, J. & Kuhn, J. (2025). On opportunities and challenges of large multimodal foundation models in education. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00301-w
title: LMFM-supported learning mechanisms for learners: multimedia feedback, barrier-free interaction, scaffolded visual and code generation, collaboration support
description: The review enumerates a set of learning mechanisms LMFM applications can facilitate for students: multimodal formative feedback combining text and images, barrier-free interaction via speech-to-text and translation, real-time scaffolding during image, handwritten-solution, and code generation, representational competence training, animation of phenomena, targeted support during experimentation, collaborative learning via peer feedback models, and interpretation of behavioral and physiological data. It notes that "text in combination with images leads to better understanding than text alone". The pattern is a learner-facing ensemble of multimodal support functions around one LMFM application.
requirements: Effective preprompting to integrate animation principles and prevent hallucinations.
Domain-specific content provided to fine-tuned LMFMs for individualized applications.
Students need sufficient representational competence to critically reflect on LMFM-generated visual representations.
constraints: Benefits for complex or abstract concepts are framed as potential; the review states LMFMs 'could' and 'may' provide these supports rather than reporting tested gains.
target_learners: students with visual or auditory impairments or difficulties in writing or reading
target_learning_goals: understanding of complex or abstract concepts
feedback during graph and code generation
examples: The review describes LMFMs analyzing images of experimental setups, generating artificial measurement data to reduce extraneous cognitive load during experimentation, and acting as conversational partners in history role-play as characters like Napoleon.

article_title: Do virtual patients prepare medical students for the real world? Development and application of a framework to compare a virtual patient collection with population data.
citation: Urresti-Gundlach M., Tolks D., Kiessling C., Wagner-Menghin M., Härtl A., Hege I. (2017). Do virtual patients prepare medical students for the real world? Development and application of a framework to compare a virtual patient collection with population data. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-1013-1
title: Collection of 66 online virtual patients in the CASUS system at LMU Munich
description: A collection of 66 online virtual patients provided as a self-directed learning module in the integrated internal medicine and operative medicine curriculum at LMU Munich, created with the CASUS® VP system by different authors and reviewed by a content matter expert and a medical educator. The VPs are "designed to match curricular objectives of common symptoms, train clinical reasoning skills, and complement the face-to-face courses."
requirements: Created with the CASUS® virtual patient system
Reviewed by a content matter expert and a medical educator
constraints: Authors were not specifically instructed to construct the VPs based on real patients or focus on common vs. rare diseases
target_learners: medical students in their second and third clinical terms
target_learning_goals: common symptoms in internal medicine and operative medicine
examples: Used as a self-directed learning module complementing lectures, problem-based learning sessions, and bedside teaching
key_sources: Urresti-Gundlach M., Tolks D., Kiessling C., Wagner-Menghin M., Härtl A., Hege I. (2017). Do virtual patients prepare medical students for the real world? Development and application of a framework to compare a virtual patient collection with population data. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-1013-1
